nameStory: This moss earned its name 'ribbed bog moss' from the distinctive grooved or ribbed appearance of its leaves when viewed up close. The scientific name Aulacomnium comes from Greek words meaning 'furrow' and 'moss,' referring to these same grooves that run along each tiny leaf like miniature valleys.
description: Ribbed bog moss is a hardy cushion-forming moss that creates dense, spongy patches in wet areas across New England. It grows in compact tufts that can reach 2-4 inches tall, with individual stems packed tightly together. The moss has a fresh green color when moist that shifts to yellowish-green or brownish when dry. Like a tiny forest of miniature trees, each stem is covered in small, overlapping leaves that give the whole patch a soft, velvety appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny leaves have distinctive lengthwise grooves or furrows that you can see with a hand lens - like microscopic corduroy fabric with parallel ridges running from base to tip

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms dense, cushion-like tufts or mats with stems packed tightly together, creating a spongy surface that springs back when gently pressed

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright to medium green when wet, becoming yellowish-green or brownish when dry - the color change is quite dramatic after rain versus drought

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels soft and velvety to the touch, with a springy, cushion-like quality that compresses under gentle finger pressure

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost always found in consistently moist to wet areas - bogs, swamps, wet meadows, and along stream edges where water is present year-round

idTips.label: Sporophytes
idTips.description: Produces thin reddish-brown stalks topped with small, cylindrical capsules that release spores - these are most visible in late spring and early summer

habitat: In New England, ribbed bog moss thrives in consistently wet environments like sphagnum bogs, cedar swamps, wet meadows, and marshy areas around ponds and streams. It prefers acidic, nutrient-poor soils and is often found growing alongside sphagnum moss, sedges, and bog plants like cranberry and pitcher plants. You'll rarely find it in dry upland areas - it needs that constant moisture to survive.

seasonality.spring: Begins producing sporophyte stalks with capsules in late spring. The moss brightens to fresh green as temperatures warm and moisture increases from snowmelt and spring rains.
seasonality.summer: Sporophyte capsules mature and release spores in early summer. During dry spells, the moss may appear brownish but quickly greens up after rain showers.
seasonality.fall: Remains visible and identifiable, though growth slows. Color may shift more toward yellowish-green as temperatures drop and daylight decreases.
seasonality.winter: Stays evergreen under snow cover, though difficult to observe when frozen. In mild winters or protected spots, the characteristic cushion form remains visible.

funFact: This tiny moss is practically a world traveler - it's found on every continent except Antarctica! Despite being less than 4 inches tall, ribbed bog moss has somehow managed to spread across the globe, growing in bogs from Alaska to New Zealand to the mountains of Venezuela.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other cushion-forming mosses in wet areas, but the ribbed leaves are the giveaway. Remember: 'Ribbed bog moss has ribbed leaves' - use a hand lens to look for those distinctive parallel grooves running lengthwise down each tiny leaf.
compareHints: Unlike its relative goose egg moss which prefers drier habitats and forms looser tufts, ribbed bog moss sticks to wet places and forms tighter cushions. Bud-headed groove-moss is much smaller and produces tiny bud-like structures instead of the tall sporophyte stalks that ribbed bog moss creates. The ribbed leaves remain the most reliable distinguishing feature among all the groove-mosses in this genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Aulacomnium relatives in New England, goose-egg moss is easily distinguished by its egg-shaped propagule clusters, which the others lack.
Unlike its relative ribbed bog moss which forms dense, tall cushions in sphagnum bogs, bud-headed groove-moss stays much smaller and looser in growth.
Unlike its relative ribbed bog moss which grows in wet, acidic bogs and has a more typical feathery moss appearance, turgid moss lives on alkaline rocky ledges and has that unmistakable swollen look.
